cases.note: §50.2: it ships with a certificate and no namespace, and belongs to nobody yet. Every finding here is a warning and none of them is a failure — a robot at the correct point in its lifecycle must not read as broken, or the first thing anybody learns about this surface is to ignore it.
cases.expected: {"attested":false,"findings":[{"code":"not_paired","message":"This robot holds no device credential, so it belongs to nobody and reports to nothing. That is the state a robot ships in (§50.2). Pair it with `skynet pair` and the code the Hub showed you.","severity":"warning","subjects":[]},{"code":"key_binding_unknown","message":"Nothing has established whether this key lives in a secure element. `security.identity.attested` is a measurement, so an unmeasured robot is reported unmeasured rather than counted as either answer.","severity":"warning","subjects":[]},{"code":"no_birth_certificate","message":"This robot holds no trusted birth certificate, so there is nothing to check the device key against. §50.3: without one, what this machine is remains a claim it makes about itself.","severity":"warning","subjects":[]}],"paired":false}

cases.note: The whole of §10 satisfied: a device credential, a namespace, a key inside a secure element, and a vendor who signed that exact key. Nothing found. The case that has to hold or every other one is measuring a function that complains about everything.

Guest tier’s ordinary state, and the ceiling §10 puts on `security.identity.attested`. A warning, because refusing it would make the tier unreachable on every machine without a TPM — which is most of them, and all of the ones anybody develops on.
cases.expected: {"attested":false,"findings":[{"code":"key_not_hardware_bound","message":"This device key is a file rather than a secret inside a secure element, so it leaves with a copy of the filesystem and identifies whatever machine that copy is put on. That is the ordinary state at guest tier and it is the ceiling §10 puts on `security.identity.attested`.","severity":"warning","subjects":[]}],"paired":true}

cases.note: Absent is not `software`. A robot nobody asked has not established it lacks a secure element, and `security.identity.attested` is a measurement — so it is reported unmeasured rather than counted as either answer.
cases.expected: {"attested":false,"findings":[{"code":"key_binding_unknown","message":"Nothing has established whether this key lives in a secure element. `security.identity.attested` is a measurement, so an unmeasured robot is reported unmeasured rather than counted as either answer.","severity":"warning","subjects":[]}],"paired":true}

cases.note: §10 pairs a robot **to a namespace**. Half a pairing is an error rather than a warning: every report this robot sends afterwards is addressed to a fleet nobody can name.
cases.expected: {"attested":true,"findings":[{"code":"namespace_missing","message":"This robot holds a credential and names no namespace. §10 pairs a robot to a namespace, so a credential without one has bound it to nothing — and every report it sends is addressed to a fleet nobody can name.","severity":"error","subjects":[]}],"paired":false}

cases.note: A user token on a robot. §10 puts the narrowest credential in the system in the field on purpose, because that is the one everybody assumes is lost — and a wider one here is a wider one lost.
cases.expected: {"attested":true,"findings":[{"code":"not_a_device_credential","message":"A device credential begins `skd_` and this one begins `skp_`. §10 puts the narrowest credential class in the system on the robot on purpose, because a credential physically present in the field is the easiest one to lose. A wider one here is a wider one lost.","severity":"error","subjects":[]}],"paired":true}

cases.note: The sentence has to work when there is nothing to quote back, which is the branch a naive format string renders as a pair of empty backticks.
cases.expected: {"attested":true,"findings":[{"code":"not_a_device_credential","message":"A device credential begins `skd_` and this one begins with nothing recognisable. §10 puts the narrowest credential class in the system on the robot on purpose, because a credential physically present in the field is the easiest one to lose. A wider one here is a wider one lost.","severity":"error","subjects":[]}],"paired":true}

cases.note: The ordinary shape of a token: the scopes live on the Hub and the robot cannot see them. A warning that says the check did not run here — which is a different sentence from saying it passed, and the difference is the whole finding.
cases.expected: {"attested":true,"findings":[{"code":"scope_undeclared","message":"This credential declares no scopes, so nothing on the robot can check that it is as narrow as §19 requires. That is the ordinary shape of an opaque bearer token and is not a fault — it means `security.credential.scope` is answered on the Hub and not here.","severity":"warning","subjects":[]}],"paired":true}

cases.note: The other direction of the allow-list, and it matters as much as the refusal: a list that rejected its own members would make every correctly issued credential an error, which is the shape of check somebody switches off.

§19’s `security.credential.scope`, from the direction that survives a rename. A deny-list of §19’s three phrases would wave through a credential that spelled repository read any other way; an allow-list refuses the spelling nobody anticipated, which is the only kind that matters.
cases.expected: {"attested":true,"findings":[{"code":"scope_unrecognised","message":"This credential carries repositories:read, which is not a capability a device credential is recognised to need. §19 assumes this credential is lost, and a capability nobody has established is narrow, on a credential everybody assumes is stolen, is refused rather than allowed.","severity":"error","subjects":["repositories:read"]}],"paired":true}

cases.note: Two of them, one repeated. The subjects list is what a console groups by, so a duplicate would render as two problems and an unsorted list would render differently on two editions.
cases.expected: {"attested":true,"findings":[{"code":"scope_unrecognised","message":"This credential carries jobs:claim, repositories:read, which is not a capability a device credential is recognised to need. §19 assumes this credential is lost, and a capability nobody has established is narrow, on a credential everybody assumes is stolen, is refused rather than allowed.","severity":"error","subjects":["jobs:claim","repositories:read"]}],"paired":true}

cases.note: The finding that only exists because §10 and §50 are both built: the key this robot was paired on is not the key its vendor signed. §50.4 says this is the expected result of a board swap and not a bug — so the message names the remedy, and the severity is still an error, because the alternative reading is a robot paired on a key nobody attested.
cases.expected: {"attested":false,"findings":[{"code":"key_not_attested","message":"The key this robot was paired on is not the key its vendor attested at manufacture. §50.2 separates what it is from whose it is, and this is the seam between them coming apart: either the mainboard was replaced — §50.4, expected, and the remedy is a vendor-signed re-issue — or this robot was paired on a key nobody signed.","severity":"error","subjects":["aa"]}],"paired":true}

cases.note: §50.3, stated as a finding: without one, what this machine is remains a claim it makes about itself. A warning — a robot with no certificate is not a robot that failed a check, it is a robot where the check could not be run.
cases.expected: {"attested":false,"findings":[{"code":"no_birth_certificate","message":"This robot holds no trusted birth certificate, so there is nothing to check the device key against. §50.3: without one, what this machine is remains a claim it makes about itself.","severity":"warning","subjects":[]}],"paired":true}

cases.note: A certificate that verified and carries no device key. Nothing to compare, so nothing is claimed — and `attested` is false, because it takes a match and not the absence of a mismatch.
The ordering of the findings, frozen. An operator who drove to a warehouse gets one list rather than one problem per attempt.

cases.note: A birth key is present and the certificate is not trusted, so there is nothing to check the key against. `attested` takes **both** halves — a hardware key nobody attested is a key the robot generated for itself — and every other case here has the certificate either trusted or the key absent, so an edition requiring only the binding agreed with this one everywhere.

cases.note: An empty list is not an absent one. Absent means an opaque bearer token whose scopes live on the Hub, which is a warning; empty means a credential that declares it carries nothing, which is nothing to refuse. An edition testing truthiness reads the first for the second and warns about a credential that said what it was.
